Surah al-Falaq is Meccan and consists of five verses.

In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾.

*Al-falaq* is on the pattern *fa'al* in the sense of *maf'ul* (the thing split or cleft). The opinions of the exegetes concerning it will come, God willing.

*Waqaba al-layl* means the night grew dark. *Waqaba al-shams* means the sun set. *Waqaba al-'adhab* means the punishment descended. The poet said:

*"The punishment descended upon them, so that it was as if the fire of the scorching wind had reached them, and they were mowed down."*

*Al-nafth* is like blowing (*nafkh*) without spitting saliva. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya. It was also said that it is blowing with saliva accompanying it, as said by al-Zamakhshari. The author of *al-Lawami'* said: it is like blowing from the mouth onto the neck without any saliva. If it is with saliva, then it is *tafl* (spitting). The poet said:

*"If I recover, I did not blow upon him; and if he is lost, then he is rightly bereaved."*

﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾ ﴿and from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾.

This surah is Meccan according to the view of al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrima and Jabir. The narration of Kurayb from Ibn 'Abbas says it is Medinan, according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas as narrated by Salih, and by Qatada and a group. It was said: this is the sound view. The occasion of the revelation of the two *mu'awwidhatayn* (the two surahs of seeking refuge) was the story of the sorcery worked upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by Labid ibn al-A'sam, a Jew. It was a *juff*, and the *juff* is the sheath of the date-palm spathe, in which were the hair of his head (peace be upon him) and the teeth of his comb, and a cord tied with eleven knots, stuck with needles. Then the two *mu'awwidhatayn* were revealed to him, and whenever he recited a verse, a knot came loose. He found relief in himself until the last knot was undone, and he rose as if he had been released from a fetter.

When the surah before it (al-Ikhlas) explained the matter of divinity, this surah explains what one seeks refuge in God from, of the evil that is in the world and of the ranks of His creatures.

*Al-falaq* means the dawn. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Zayd. In the proverb it is said: "It is clearer than the *falaq* of the dawn and the *faraq* of the dawn." The poet said:

*"O night that I did not sleep, I spent it watching, tending the stars until the dawn was decreed."*

The poet describing the wild bull said:

*"Until, when the dawn cleared from its face, its guide was standing in the last part of the night."*

It was also said: *al-falaq* is everything that God splits, such as the earth for plants, mountains for springs, clouds for rain, wombs for offspring, grain and date-stones, and other things. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did a group of the Companions and the Successors: *al-falaq* is a pit in Hell. This was narrated by Abu Hurayra from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said: it is what is deepest in the earth, and its plural is *fulqan*. It was also said: it is a valley in Hell. One of the Companions said: it is a house in Hell, which when opened, all the people of the Fire cry out because of its intense heat.

The majority read ﴿min sharri ma khalaq﴾ with *sharr* in the genitive construction with *ma*. *Ma* is general and includes everything in which evil is found, of animate beings that are accountable, and of those that are not, and of inanimate things, such as burning by fire, drowning in the sea, and killing by poison.

'Amr ibn Fa'id read *min sharrin* with *tanwin* (nunation). 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and some of the Mu'tazila (a theological school who held that God does not create evil), said Ibn 'Atiyya, read *min sharrin* with *tanwin*, and *ma khalaq* as a negation. This *qira'a* (recitation variant) is rejected and based on a false doctrine, since God is the Creator of everything. Yet this recitation has a possibility other than negation, which is that *ma khalaq* is a substitute (*badal*) for *sharrin* with an omitted element, meaning: "from the evil of the evil of what He created." The second *sharr* was omitted because the first *sharr* indicates it. He spoke in general first, then specified second. So it should not be rejected.

*Al-ghasiq* is the night, and *waqaba* means it grew dark and entered upon people. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. Al-Zamakhshari criticised this, as is his habit, and said: "*Al-ghasiq* is the night when its darkness thickens, from His saying: ﴿to the darkness of the night﴾ [al-Isra 78]. From it: *ghasaqat al-'ayn* means the eye filled with tears, and *ghasaqat al-jirahah* means the wound filled with blood. Its *wuqub* is the entry of its darkness into everything." End of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the night, because it is colder than the day, and *al-ghasiq* means the cold. One seeks refuge from its evil because in it the devils, the venomous creatures, insects and those who commit murder spread. The poet said:

*"O phantom of Hind, you have left me sleepless, when you came to us by night while the night had grown dark."*

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: the day has entered into the night. Ibn Shihab (al-Zuhri) said: the intended meaning of *al-ghasiq* is the sun when it sets. al-Qutabi and others said: it is the moon when it enters its *sahur* (eclipse shadow) and is eclipsed. In a hadith: the Prophet (ﷺ) looked at the moon and said: "O 'A'isha, we seek refuge in God from this, for it is the *ghasiq* when it *waqaba*." And from him (ﷺ): "The *ghasiq* is the star." Ibn Zayd said, citing the Arabs: the *ghasiq* is the Pleiades (*al-Thurayya*) when it sets, and diseases and plague then spread. It was also said: it is the snake when it bites, and the *ghasiq* is the poison of its fang, because it flows from it.

*Al-naffathat* are women, or souls, or the groups of female sorcerers who tie knots in threads and blow upon them and recite charms. The majority read *al-naffathat*. Al-Hasan read it with a *damma* on the *nun* (*al-nuffathat*). Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan also, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim and Ya'qub in one narration read *al-nafithat*. Al-Hasan also and Abu al-Rabi' read *al-naffathat* without the *alif*, like *al-khaddarat*. Seeking refuge from their evil means seeking refuge from the harm that God inflicts upon them when they do such deeds.

The occasion of the revelation of these two *mu'awwidhatayn* refutes what al-Zamakhshari interpreted from the saying (of God): "It may be that by it is meant the women of wiles, from His saying: ﴿Indeed your guile is great﴾ [Yusuf 28], comparing their guile to sorcery and blowing into knots; or those who tempt men by exposing themselves to them and displaying their beauty, as if they bewitch them with that." End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: this blowing is into knots tied in threads and the like, in the name of the bewitched person, so that he is harmed thereby. This practice is widespread in our time in the deserts of the Maghrib. A trustworthy person told me that he saw with some people a red thread in which knots had been tied over foals, so that they were prevented from suckling their mothers. Whenever a knot was untied, that foal would immediately run to its mother and suckle. End of quote.

It was said: *al-ghasiq* is the envier by the eye, because if the night does not enter, it is not attributed to him. Likewise everything that *al-ghasiq* was interpreted as, and likewise the envier: his envy has no effect if he does not show it, by plotting against the envied in what harms him. But if the envy is not displayed, then it harms only him, not the envied, because of his distress at another's blessing. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also possible that by the evil of the envier is meant his sin, and the ugliness of his state at the time of his envy and the display of its effect. End of quote.

He generalised first, saying ﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾, then specified these because their evil is hidden, as it comes from where it is not known. They said: "The worst of enemies is the one who lures with your guile from where you do not perceive."

He used indefinite forms for *ghasiq* and *hasid*, and the definite form for *al-naffathat*, because every *naffathah* is evil, whereas every *ghasiq* does not have evil in it; evil is found only in some and not in others. Likewise, not every envier harms, and there is envy that is praiseworthy, which is envy in good things. From this is the saying: "There is no envy except in two (matters)." From it is the verse of Abu Tammam:

*"And one who envies in noble deeds is no (true) envier."*

Another said:

*"Indeed, glory looks good with envy of its like."*

And the saying of the one being looked at to the envier, when he gazes upon him: "Five upon your eyes", meaning by it this surah, because it has five verses. The evil eye of the envier is, for the most part, effective. We seek refuge in God from its evil.

The poet describing the wild bull said:
